displayQuote: America is great because America is good, and if America ever ceases to be good, America will cease to be great

meta.title: Who really said "America is great because America is good, and if America ever ceases to be good, America will cease to be great"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Alexis de Tocqueville never wrote it. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed; the passage is documented in print by 1922, with an 1886 sermon ancestor.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'America is great because America is good, and if America ever ceases to be good, America will cease to be great'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Tocqueville. The line is absent from Democracy in America; Wikiquote documents it in print by 1922, author unknown. Nixon and Reagan spread it.

answer.label: Not Alexis de Tocqueville — an unsourced sermon passage
answer.authorDates: Author unknown · documented in print by 1922
answer.sourceLine: The sentence appears nowhere in Democracy in America. Wikiquote files it under Misattributed, noting it “has often been attributed to de Tocqueville’s Democracy in America, but erroneously” — and a full-text search of the Henry Reeve translation of both volumes turns up none of the passage’s distinctive language. The earliest printing Wikiquote documents is in the Herald and Presbyter of 6 September 1922 — where, as Barry Popik’s transcription shows, a Labor Day sermon by Rev. John McDowell already credits it to Tocqueville. Looser ancestors run back to an 1886 sermon collection and, further still, to an 1836 English travel narrative. No author has been established, and the candidates put forward disagree.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Henry Reeve translation, volumes 1 and 2 (Project Gutenberg 815, 816) — passage absent
Herald and Presbyter, 6 September 1922, p. 8 — already credited to Tocqueville there
Madison Clinton Peters, Empty Pews & Selections from Other Sermons on Timely Topics (Zeising, 1886), p. 35
The Methodist Review, 1908 — the same set-piece, credited to Tocqueville (per Barry Popik)
Andrew Reed & James Matheson, A Narrative of the Visit to the American Churches, 2nd ed. (London, 1836), vol. 2, p. 226

source.excerpt: In the end, the state of the Union comes down to the character of the people. I sought for the greatness and genius of America in her commodious harbors and her ample rivers, and it was not there. In the fertile fields and boundless prairies, and it was not there. In her rich mines and her vast world commerce, and it was not there. Not until I went into the churches of America and heard her pulpits, aflame with righteousness, did I understand the secret of her genius and power. America is great because she is good, and if America ever ceases to be good, America will cease to be great.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ lists the sentence in its Misattributed section for Tocqueville and says it “has often been attributed to de Tocqueville’s Democracy in America, but erroneously.” Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation, so Wikiquote is the standing research anchor.

The book itself settles it. The full Henry Reeve translation is on Project Gutenberg ↗ (volume 1; volume 2 is eBook 816). Searching both volumes returns zero hits for “pulpit,” “aflame,” “cease to be great,” “ceases to be good” and “America is great.”

For the chronology, Wikiquote ↗ documents the passage in the Herald and Presbyter of 6 September 1922, p. 8, and an ending-less variant in Madison Clinton Peters’ sermon collection of 1886, p. 35. Wikiquote gives dates only; for what the 1922 item actually says, Barry Popik ↗ transcribes it — “Dr. McDowell closed his message with the quotation from Alexis de Tocqueville” — and adds a 1908 Methodist Review appearance between the 1886 and 1922 dates.

The article Wikiquote leans on is still readable: John J. Pitney Jr., “The Tocqueville Fraud” ↗, The Weekly Standard, 13 November 1995 (now archived at the Washington Examiner). Pitney traces the modern spread to a 1941 book on religion and the American dream that quoted the closing lines as Tocqueville’s with no documentation — its author, he suggests, “may have mistaken his own notes for a verbatim quotation” — and then to an Eisenhower campaign speech of about 1952, whose writer hedged the credit to “a wise philosopher.” Note that Pitney’s chain starts in 1941, and the printings above are older still, so it explains the line’s modern career rather than its origin.

For how it spread, the American Presidency Project ↗ returns seven documents, from Nixon in 1970 to Ford in 1996. Nixon introduced it as something “Alexis de Tocqueville, observing America more than a century ago, wrote.”
source.excerptNote: The expanded passage as Wikiquote records it. Note the ending: this longer form runs “America is great because she is good,” while the compact form Hillary Clinton used in 2016 runs “America is great because America is good.” The presidents in the record below all used the “she” wording. Neither version is in Tocqueville.

source.rightsNote: No author and no original work have been identified for this passage, so there is nothing to which a copyright — or a public-domain status — can honestly be traced, and quotle.info asserts none. The earliest printing on record, in the Herald and Presbyter of 6 September 1922, predates the 1931 US cutoff, but that is a fact about one magazine issue, not about the sentence’s unknown source.

author.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: Alexis de Tocqueville — who did not write it
author.metaLine: 1805–1859 · French political thinker, magistrate and author of Democracy in America
author.bio: Tocqueville was a French magistrate, political philosopher and historian who arrived in the United States in 1831 nominally to study its prisons and turned the journey into Democracy in America, published in 1835 and 1840. Religion and manners genuinely are among his recurring subjects — both volumes return them on page after page — which is precisely why an invented sentence about American churches sounds so plausible in his mouth. It is still not his.

misattribution.heading: Four things go wrong at once
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-quoted sentences in American public life and one of the most reliably wrong. The book it is credited to does not contain it, and no one has established an author for it — the candidates that have been put forward disagree with each other.

items.who: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America (1835, 1840)
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ files the sentence under Misattributed and states it “has often been attributed to de Tocqueville’s Democracy in America, but erroneously.” Searching the full Henry Reeve translation of both volumes on Project Gutenberg ↗ returns nothing for “pulpit,” “aflame,” “cease to be great” or “America is great” — and its one use of “commodious” describes army promotion, not harbors.

items.who: The Herald and Presbyter, 1922 — already crediting Tocqueville
items.why: The passage’s earliest documented printing, in the Herald and Presbyter of 6 September 1922, p. 8, already credits it to Tocqueville — Rev. John McDowell closed a Labor Day sermon with it. Barry Popik ↗ transcribes the item: “Dr. McDowell closed his message with the quotation from Alexis de Tocqueville, as follows: ‘I sought for the greatness and genius of America in her commodious harbors…’” Wikiquote ↗ dates the passage to at least 1922 and says nothing about how it was credited; it does not identify a real author. So the oldest exhibit on record is the oldest recorded misattribution, not an anonymous first appearance.

items.who: Reed and Matheson 1836, Madison Clinton Peters 1886, the Methodist Review 1908
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ points to an earlier variant “without the memorable ending” in Empty Pews & Selections from Other Sermons on Timely Topics (Zeising, 1886), p. 35, in which a traveller searches America’s markets, courts and legislative halls in vain and finds the answer only on entering the church. Peters is not identified as the author of the later wording. Two more antecedents sit outside Wikiquote’s account: Barry Popik ↗ records the same set-piece in the Methodist Review in 1908, and the historian Robert Tracy McKenzie ↗ argues the seed is fifty years older than Peters — the English ministers Andrew Reed and James Matheson, who toured America in 1834 and wrote “America will be great if America is good. If not, her greatness will vanish away like a morning cloud” (A Narrative of the Visit to the American Churches, 2nd ed., London, 1836, vol. 2, p. 226). Different researchers therefore point at different starting lines.

items.who: Nixon, Reagan, Bush, Ford — and Eisenhower, Clinton, Powell, Perot, Buchanan
items.why: The American Presidency Project ↗ returns the line from Nixon in 1970 through Ford in 1996; Reagan’s radio address of 24 May 1986 says flatly, “de Tocqueville concluded that America is great, because she is good.” Wikiquote ↗ additionally records Michael A. Ledeen’s account in Tocqueville on American Character (2001), p. 25, that Dwight Eisenhower, Bill Clinton, Colin Powell, Ross Perot and Pat Buchanan each credited it to Tocqueville, and notes Hillary Clinton used the “America is good” form in her acceptance speech of 29 July 2016 without attribution.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has produced the sentence in anything Tocqueville wrote, and no author has been established for it — the candidates put forward run from an 1836 English travel narrative to an undocumented 1941 devotional book, and they disagree. What is firmly documented is a sermon-style passage in print by 1922, already misattributed, with looser ancestors in 1908 and 1886 — see Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ and Barry Popik’s citation list ↗.

context.heading: A bipartisan misquote
lead: It sounds exactly like Tocqueville, which is the whole problem: a French visitor tours the young republic and delivers a verdict on the source of its strength. But the passage that carries the sentence is a pulpit set-piece, not travel writing — a narrator marching past harbors, prairies, mines and commerce and finding the secret only when he steps into a church. Tocqueville really did write at length about religion and manners in America, and that plausibility is exactly what has kept the counterfeit in circulation.

The line has been quoted from the highest platforms in American life, by both parties. The American Presidency Project ↗ returns it in Richard Nixon’s statement of 24 October 1970, Ronald Reagan’s remarks in March and August 1984 and his radio address of 24 May 1986, George Bush’s remarks of 10 October 1991, the 1992 Republican Party platform and Gerald Ford’s 1996 convention address. Wikiquote records Hillary Clinton using the “America is good” form in her convention acceptance speech of 29 July 2016, without attributing it to anyone.
detailsBody: The Henry Reeve translation of Democracy in America is available in full from Project Gutenberg as eBooks 815 (volume 1) and 816 (volume 2). Searching both files for the passage’s distinctive words returns nothing: “pulpit,” “aflame,” “cease to be great,” “ceases to be good” and “America is great” each appear zero times. The word “commodious” occurs exactly once, in volume 2, describing the slow advancement of a peacetime army — not harbors.

The 1886 ancestor Wikiquote points to has the same architecture but no punchline: a traveller passes through thoroughfares of trade, mountains, valleys, manufactories, markets, courts and legislative halls, and finds the secret of American success only on entering the church. The memorable good-and-great ending is not there. Whoever welded that ending on has not been established — and the researchers who have tried do not agree on where to start. Barry Popik puts another instance in the Methodist Review in 1908; the historian Robert Tracy McKenzie reaches back fifty years before Peters to the English ministers Andrew Reed and James Matheson, who toured America in 1834 and wrote “America will be great if America is good. If not, her greatness will vanish away like a morning cloud” (2nd ed., London, 1836, vol. 2, p. 226); and John Pitney’s 1995 account starts later still, with an undocumented 1941 devotional book. We have not been able to close the gap between them.
context.pull: It is in every speechwriter’s drawer — and in neither volume of the book it is credited to.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Alexis de Tocqueville. The true author is not established; no creator is asserted here. The earliest documented printing is the Herald and Presbyter of 6 September 1922, p. 8, which is where the passage was first recorded — already credited to Tocqueville — not a source work it came from.
